snippet.title: The Cactus Magazine - Chrome Dino IRL part 3
snippet.description:
The Cactus Magazine - Chrome Dino IRL Part 3
•••
The obstacles magnet onto the 3D printed conveyor belt, and if they just rode around in a loop the game would be the same sequence forever. So at the end of the belt, these ramps passively pull each obstacle off and drop it into a ten-sided indexing wheel. Every drop ratchets the wheel forward one slot, which pushes the next obstacle up to the top of the queue, ready to go back into the game.
•••
The original plan was a gantry-style pick-and-place that would grab obstacles and set them on the moving belt, but the obstacles are all different sizes, so it would've needed a vision system just to find them, plus a gripper synced to a moving conveyor. The indexing wheel does the same job with fewer moving parts.
•••
The end goal is three of these magazines side by side with a randomizer picking which one serves up the next obstacle, so the sequence never repeats. Stay tuned for that!
•••
#engineezy #engineering #mechanicalengineering #mechanisms #chromedino

snippet.title: Bro really parked THIS close 😭
snippet.description:
This starts off looking like a completely ordinary parking lot moment — just a bright blue Porsche sitting perfectly inside its lines while someone points at it like something is wrong. At first, it feels like another clip where people overreact about expensive cars taking up space or parking weirdly. Everything makes it seem like the Porsche is the one being judged. But then the camera slowly reveals what’s actually going on, and the whole situation flips. The car isn’t the problem at all… it’s the tiny scooter parked ridiculously close next to it, almost like it claimed the spot on purpose. Suddenly, the perspective changes, and the clip turns from criticism into pure irony, making the ending hit way harder than expected. 💀🚗

snippet.title: The offleash teenager strikes AGAIN?! #viral #servicedogs #dogtraining #dogs #shorts #fyp #walmart
snippet.description:
I was just minding my business in the craft section with my service dog when suddenly an off-leash teenager dramatically slides across the floor, pets my service dog, and runs away. Absolutely crazy behavior. 😂

Now, on a serious note, because I already know people are going to jump straight to the comments without reading the caption: YES, this is a skit. More specifically, it’s a training skit.

The “off-leash teenager” is my little brother, and these scenarios are something we intentionally practice with Fidget. As you can see in the video, Fidget barely reacts. He doesn’t flinch, move away, break position, or lose focus on me. He watches what’s happening because obviously he’s aware of his surroundings, but he remains calm and focused.

That’s because we practice weird, dramatic, unpredictable scenarios like this.

A lot of my “off-leash child” and “off-leash teenager” skits are actually inspired by things I’ve experienced while working service dogs in public. Once I experience something, I like to recreate a controlled version of it so I know my dogs are prepared if something similar happens again.

Have I ever had a child dramatically slide across the floor and pet Fidget? No. 😂 But I HAVE had children run up to him, jump around him, fall near him, reach for him, pet him, and run away. So why not add another ridiculous scenario to our training?

The goal is never to scare or overwhelm my service dog. It’s to safely expose him to unusual situations in a controlled environment so that if something unpredictable happens in real life, I already know he can remain calm, comfortable, and focused.

These videos do have an educational purpose as well. Kids DO approach service dogs. Teenagers DO sometimes intentionally mess with service dogs. And sometimes parents simply aren’t paying attention or don’t tell their children that approaching or touching someone else’s dog isn’t okay.

So please teach your kids about service animals. Teach your teenagers that harassing or distracting a service animal isn’t funny. And remember that it is perfectly okay to tell your child “no.”

Your child does not need to touch every dog they see. They do not need to approach every dog they see. And they especially should not be interfering with a service animal that is actively working.

The ridiculous training scenarios have a very real purpose.

#servicedogs #viral #dogs #teens #fyp
